events.headline: Disney swallows ABC
events.text:
Five weeks into the tank, Disney closes its purchase of Capital Cities/ABC, owner of the ABC network and 80 percent of ESPN, for $19 billion. When it was announced, the Baltimore Sun called it the largest merger ever in the entertainment industry.
Disney comes out of it worth $40 billion. Watch the phone companies below: they are about to start eating each other.

events.headline: The Bells put themselves back together
events.text:
Bell Atlantic eats GTE for $53 billion and renames itself Verizon. Three years earlier it had swallowed NYNEX. On the same day Qwest, a fiber upstart that only went public in 1997, eats US West.
SBC has been just as hungry: Pacific Telesis in 1997, Ameritech in 1999. Verizon is now worth $118 billion, SBC $149 billion.

events.headline: The guppy eats the whale
events.text:
AOL, worth about $2.2 billion when the tank opened in 1996, closes its purchase of Time Warner, a deal valued at $182 billion when it was announced a year earlier. It is the largest deal in this tank, before or since.
In January 2003, the merged company reported a loss of $99 billion, the largest ever for a corporation at the time.

events.minor: AT&T spins off AT&T Wireless
Netflix, a DVD-by-mail company, goes public as a guppy

events.headline: WorldCom goes belly up
events.text:
WorldCom, which had eaten MCI four years earlier for $37 billion, files for bankruptcy after an accounting scandal. It is the largest bankruptcy filing in US history at the time.
At its last annual report before the boom ended it was worth $180 billion. It will come back in 2004 under MCI's name.

events.headline: AT&T comes apart, and Comcast feeds
events.text:
Having paid $48 billion for TCI in 1999 and $62 billion for MediaOne in 2000, AT&T gives up on cable. Its cable unit pops off and Comcast swallows it in a deal valued at $72 billion.
Comcast had been worth $4.5 billion in 1996. Now it is $66 billion. AT&T, already short its wireless arm, is down to $15 billion.

events.headline: The child eats the parent
events.text:
SBC, the smallest of the Baby Bells split off from AT&T in 1984, buys its old parent for $16 billion and takes its name. At the start of 1996 AT&T Corp. was worth $104 billion. At its last annual report before the sale it was worth $12 billion.
The new AT&T is worth $95 billion. A year later it eats BellSouth too.

events.headline: The phone company buys Hollywood
events.text:
AT&T, which had already eaten DirecTV, buys Time Warner, the company AOL swallowed in 2001. Wikipedia's list of the largest acquisitions puts the deal at $85 billion, or more including debt.
AT&T is now a phone company, a satellite TV company and a movie studio, worth $232 billion.

events.headline: Disney eats most of Fox
events.text:
21st Century Fox pops. Most of it goes to Disney, in a deal valued at $71 billion. What is left swims off as a new, smaller company, Fox Corp.
Disney has now swallowed ABC, Pixar, Marvel, Lucasfilm and most of Fox, and is worth $244 billion.

events.headline: AT&T spits Time Warner back out
events.text:
Four years after buying it, AT&T gives up on Hollywood. WarnerMedia pops out of AT&T and Discovery, the cable channel company, swallows it, a deal valued at $43 billion. The combined fish is Warner Bros. Discovery.
AT&T goes back to being a phone company, worth $152 billion. Netflix, a guppy that went public in 2002, is worth $155 billion.

events.headline: The smallest studio eats the biggest
events.text:
Paramount Skydance, worth $11 billion on the stock market, closes its $111 billion purchase of Warner Bros. Discovery after outbidding Netflix, and renames itself Skydance. Warner Bros. Discovery was worth $78 billion just before.
The Warner Bros. studio has now been inside four fish in this tank: Time Warner, AOL Time Warner, AT&T and Warner Bros. Discovery, and Skydance makes five.

gaps: The tank starts in January 1996. No free source we could reach gives market values for these companies before then, so the 1984 breakup of the Bell System, Time Inc. and Warner Communications (1990) and Capital Cities buying ABC (1985) happen before the first frame.

Firms that no longer trade are sized from the cover of each annual report, which gives the value of shares held by outside investors on one date a year. That leaves out shares held by insiders, so a few fish are drawn smaller than their full stock-market value, most of all Charter before 2009 (Paul Allen's class B shares are excluded) and Pixar (Steve Jobs's stake is excluded).

Viacom, the second Viacom and News Corp / 21st Century Fox have voting and non-voting shares. For them the value is every class's shares outstanding times that class's price, both printed on the annual report cover; share counts are from a few weeks after the price date.

AOL Time Warner's first annual report cover after the merger is dated February 2002, so between the January 2001 merger and then its size is eased from AOL's last value before the deal. Its real 2001 value is not shown.
Turner Broadcasting (bought by Time Warner in October 1996) is left out: we found no deal value or full market value for it in the sources used.
Bright House Networks, bought together with Time Warner Cable in 2016, is left out because the sources give one price for both.

News Corp is in the tank only from November 2004, when it moved from Australia to the US and began filing US annual reports. Before that it filed as a foreign company and its covers carry no US market value.

Cox Communications, public until Cox Enterprises took it private in December 2004, is left out of those years: its annual reports give a value only for the Class A shares held by outside investors, a small slice of the company. It appears only when Charter buys it in 2026, sized by the deal.

Left out entirely: NCR (spun off by AT&T in 1996, a computer maker), Time Inc. (2014 spin-off from Time Warner), Cablevision, Dish Network, Sirius XM and Cingular Wireless (owned by SBC and BellSouth, never traded on its own). AT&T's 2021 move of DirecTV into a venture with TPG, and its 2025 sale of the rest, are not shown.

Wikipedia's list of the largest deals gives $52 billion for Bell Atlantic and NYNEX (announced 1996). That figure may describe the size of the combined company rather than the price paid; we use it as listed.

Deal values are as reported in the sources, which sometimes include the target's debt and sometimes don't. They are in dollars of the day; the predator rule converts them to today's dollars with the consumer price index.

After Paramount Skydance closed its purchase of Warner Bros. Discovery on October 6, 2026, the monthly source had not yet updated Skydance's share count, so its size in the last weeks of the tank may be too small.
Bright House was part of the 2016 deal but has no price of its own in the sources, so it isn't drawn.
GTE: first value is 1997-01-02, so it is drawn at that size from 1996-01-01.
WorldCom: first value is 1997-01-02, so it is drawn at that size from 1996-01-01.
Nextel: first value is 1997-03-01, so it is drawn at that size from 1996-01-01.
AT&T Wireless: first value is 2002-02-28, so it is drawn at that size from 2001-07-15.
MediaOne: first value is 1999-02-26, so it is drawn at that size from 1998-06-18.
Charter: first value is 2001-01-31, so it is drawn at that size from 1999-11-03.
DirecTV: first value is 2004-06-30, so it is drawn at that size from 2003-12-22.
AOL: first value is 1996-08-31, so it is drawn at that size from 1996-01-01.
21st Century Fox: first value is 2013-12-31, so it is drawn at that size from 2013-06-28.
Pixar: first value is 1997-03-20, so it is drawn at that size from 1996-01-01.
Marvel: first value is 1997-01-02, so it is drawn at that size from 1996-01-01.
SBC on 2000-03-06: monthly value $121 billion is below the $147 billion the company reported for shares held by outside investors alone.

text.value_method: Values come from three kinds of source. For companies that still trade, or traded into the 2000s, companiesmarketcap.com gives a market value at the end of each month (for the last two years, each week). For companies that no longer trade, the value is read off the cover of each annual report filed with the SEC. For the few companies with no stock price of their own, the size is the price paid in a deal, or the value implied when a known slice of the company was sold; these are drawn as dashed outlines. Where the monthly source and the SEC covers overlap, the build checks one against the other; the monthly source was wrong for Comcast before its 2002 AT&T Broadband deal and counted only one of Sprint's two stocks before 2005, so SEC covers are used there instead.
text.species_method: Species follow two rules. A fish becomes a predator, and stays one, on its second purchase worth $1 billion or more in today's dollars (2026 prices, using the consumer price index for September 2026). Below $10 billion in today's dollars a fish is drawn as a guppy; above it, as a grown fish.
text.intro: January 1996. Five of the seven Baby Bells split off from AT&T in 1984 are still on their own, and so is their old parent. Disney is five weeks from closing its purchase of ABC.
text.end: Of the 14 phone companies swimming in January 1996, 3 are still here: SBC (now AT&T), Bell Atlantic (now Verizon), CenturyTel (now Lumen). The biggest fish in the tank now: Netflix ($293 billion), Disney ($190 billion), Verizon ($182 billion), T-Mobile US ($167 billion). Netflix never ate anything in this tank. It swam in at $311 million in May 2002 and grew on its own.
